prompt: In symmetric cryptography, which key decrypts a file that was encrypted with key K?
hint: The name says it.

choices.text: A second key derived from K by the cipher
choices.why: No second key exists in a symmetric scheme.

choices.text: K itself
choices.why: Right: one key, both directions.

choices.text: The public half of K's key pair
choices.why: Key pairs belong to asymmetric cryptography, lesson 2.

choices.text: Any key of the same length as K
choices.why: A key of the right length is still the wrong key; the lab's aes-256-b failed.

prompt: Decrypting `referral.enc` with `aes-256-b.hex` printed `bad decrypt`. What did OpenSSL actually detect?
hint: It is not the key that is checked.

choices.text: That the key was not the one used to encrypt
choices.why: AES has no way to recognise its own key.

choices.text: That the IV did not match the ciphertext
choices.why: The IV was the right one; only the key changed.

choices.text: That the padding was invalid
choices.why: Right: a check on the padding, which some wrong keys pass by chance.

choices.text: That the file had been altered after encryption
choices.why: Nothing was altered; and plain CBC cannot tell anyway.

prompt: Vereda's developer wants to keep the AES algorithm secret as an extra layer. What does Kerckhoffs's principle say?
hint: What is the only secret?

choices.text: Security must not depend on hiding the algorithm
choices.why: Right: a secret algorithm leaks and has not been examined.

choices.text: Algorithms should be kept secret and keys made public
choices.why: It is the reverse.

choices.text: Keep both secret, as defence in depth
choices.why: A secret algorithm adds no strength and hides flaws from reviewers.

choices.text: Use a 512-bit key instead of hiding it
choices.why: AES has no 512-bit key, and the principle is not about length.

prompt: The lab's `aes-256.hex` holds how many hexadecimal digits?
hint: Two digits per byte.

prompt: What is the block size of AES-256?
hint: The key size does not change it.

choices.text: 256 bits
choices.why: That is the key, not the block.

choices.text: 128 bits
choices.why: Right: every AES variant uses 16-byte blocks.

choices.text: 64 bits
choices.why: That was DES's block.

choices.text: It depends on the mode
choices.why: The mode decides how blocks are chained, not their size.

prompt: A 300-byte file is encrypted with AES-CBC and PKCS#7 padding. How long is the ciphertext, not counting the IV?
A 4,096-byte file is encrypted with AES-CBC and PKCS#7 padding. How long is the ciphertext, not counting the IV?
hint: 4,096 is already a multiple of 16.

prompt: Why does PKCS#7 add a whole block when the data already fills the last one?
hint: Think of a file that ends in the byte 01.

choices.text: To make the ciphertext longer and harder to guess
choices.why: Length adds no secrecy.

choices.text: Because AES refuses a block that is all data
choices.why: AES encrypts any 16 bytes.

choices.text: So that removing padding is never ambiguous
choices.why: Right: otherwise data ending in 01 would look padded.

choices.text: To hold the IV for the next message
choices.why: The IV travels separately, at the start.

prompt: Encrypted with ECB, the appointment file still showed which slots were booked. Why?
hint: Compare the plaintext letters with the ciphertext letters.

choices.text: The key was too short for the file
choices.why: The key was 256 bits; length was not the problem.

choices.text: Equal blocks stayed equal
choices.why: Right: ECB encrypts each block alone.

choices.text: AES leaks the first bytes of each block
choices.why: AES leaks nothing about a single block.

choices.text: The padding block revealed the record size
choices.why: The pattern was in all 32 blocks, not the last.

prompt: Encrypted with CTR, the 512-byte appointment file gave 32 blocks, while CBC gave 33. Why the difference?
hint: What does CTR actually pass through AES?

choices.text: CTR compresses repeated blocks
choices.why: No mode compresses anything.

choices.text: CTR stores the IV inside the last block
choices.why: The IV is not in the ciphertext count here.

choices.text: CTR turns AES into a stream, so it needs no padding
choices.why: Right: the stream is cut to the data's length.

choices.text: CBC adds a block for its integrity check
choices.why: Plain CBC has no integrity check; the extra block is padding.

prompt: Match each mode to what describes it.
hint: One description fits no mode of this section.

pairs.right: each block encrypted on its own
each block mixed with the previous ciphertext block
a counter encrypted into a keystream

right_distractors: a key that changes every block

prompt: A database stores each patient's blood type, encrypted on its own with AES in ECB under one key. What can somebody with read access and no key learn?
hint: Each value is less than one block.

choices.text: Nothing, because each value fits in one block
choices.why: One block per value is exactly where ECB's equality shows.

choices.text: Which patients share a blood type
choices.why: Right: equal values give equal ciphertexts, and the most common one is easy to name.

choices.text: The key, given enough rows
choices.why: Equality leaks; the key does not.

choices.text: Every blood type, since AES is reversible
choices.why: Reversible only with the key.

prompt: Is an initialisation vector a secret?
hint: Decryption needs it.

choices.text: Yes, it is as secret as the key and stored apart from it
choices.why: It travels in the open beside the ciphertext.

choices.text: No, but it must be fresh each time
choices.why: Right: public, fresh for each message.

choices.text: No, so one constant IV for every message is fine
choices.why: A constant IV gave two identical ciphertexts in the lab.

choices.text: Only in GCM, where it doubles as the key
choices.why: In no mode is it secret.

prompt: The letter was encrypted twice with `iv-a` and the two SHA-256 fingerprints matched. What does that let an observer learn?
hint: They have no key.

choices.text: The full text of the referral letter
choices.why: Without the key, the text stays hidden.

choices.text: The key, by comparing the two ciphertexts
choices.why: Two equal ciphertexts reveal nothing about the key.

choices.text: That both messages were identical
choices.why: Right: equality is the leak.

choices.text: Nothing that matters
choices.why: Equality of messages is information.

prompt: A GCM nonce does not have to be random, but under one key it must be ___.
hint: A counter satisfies it.

prompt: A service encrypts with AES-GCM, using a counter kept in memory as the nonce. After each restart the counter starts at 1 again. What is wrong?
hint: Same key, before and after the restart.

choices.text: Nothing: a counter is an acceptable nonce
choices.why: A counter is acceptable only while it never repeats.

choices.text: The nonce must be secret, and a counter is guessable
choices.why: Guessable is fine for GCM; repeated is not.

choices.text: After a restart, nonces 1, 2, 3 recur under the same key
choices.why: Right: the counter must survive restarts, or the key must change.

choices.text: GCM needs a 16-byte nonce, not a counter
choices.why: GCM uses 12-byte nonces, and a counter fits.

prompt: One bit of `slots.gcm` was changed and `vcrypt open` ran with the right key. What did it return?
hint: Look at the exit status.

choices.text: The file with one slot garbled
choices.why: That is what an unauthenticated mode would do.

choices.text: The first slots, then an error
choices.why: GCM checks before it returns anything.

choices.text: Nothing, and an authentication failure
choices.why: Right: the tag did not match.

choices.text: The original file, repaired by the tag
choices.why: A tag detects; it does not repair.

prompt: Why did Vereda pass `--aad patient=4471` when sealing the referral letter?
hint: The id is not encrypted.

choices.text: To encrypt the patient id along with the letter
choices.why: Associated data is checked, not encrypted.

choices.text: So it cannot be moved to another patient
choices.why: Right: opened with patient=5120, it failed.

choices.text: Because GCM needs extra entropy
choices.why: The nonce and key supply what GCM needs.

choices.text: To make the tag shorter
choices.why: The tag is 16 bytes either way.

prompt: A program decrypts a record and gets an authentication failure. Which reactions are correct? Choose all that apply.
hint: The data is to be treated as absent.

choices.text: Refuse the record and show none of it
choices.why: Yes: nothing that failed the tag is trusted.

choices.text: Log the failure as an event worth looking at
choices.why: Yes: a failure may be an attack or a fault.

choices.text: Try the older keys until one decrypts
choices.why: Trying keys until one passes turns the check into a guessing game.

choices.text: Show the part that decrypted before the error
choices.why: GCM returns no part, and none should be shown.

prompt: Put the decisions of this lesson in the order a developer makes them when encrypting a file.
hint: The key first, the check last.
items: draw a fresh nonce for this file
encrypt and store the nonce and tag with it
on reading, refuse it if the tag fails

prompt: Match each failure to the decision that would have prevented it.
hint: Each one is a section of this lesson.

pairs.left: booked slots readable through the ciphertext
two equal letters giving equal ciphertexts
an altered record decrypted without complaint
a ciphertext copied into another patient's row
pairs.right: the patient id as associated data

prompt: A colleague proposes AES-256-CBC with a random IV for a new backup format, with no other check. What is the strongest objection?
hint: Confidentiality is covered.

choices.text: 256-bit keys are too slow for backups
choices.why: Speed is not the problem with this design.

choices.text: A random IV leaks the date the backup was taken
choices.why: An IV is random bytes and carries no date.

choices.text: CBC shows the pattern of repeated blocks
choices.why: That is ECB; CBC hides repetition.

choices.text: Nothing would detect a backup altered on disk
choices.why: Right: use GCM, or add a MAC over the ciphertext.
